title: Equilibrium with Momentum
keywords: Bill of Rights vs prosperity provisions
primary_topics: Remarks at the book launch of 'Momentum: Economic Reforms for Sustaining Growth,' October 23, 2019 -- praising the five economist-authors as the equivalent of a Supreme Court for economic matters
The 'legal equilibrium' thesis: CJP's liberty-and-prosperity philosophy is in equilibrium with the economists' thesis, but viewed from a lawyer's lenses rather than an economist's

The Tanada v. Angara WTO decision (1997): the landmark case where CJP convinced all 14 colleagues -- after beginning with only three concurrers -- to unanimously uphold the Philippines' WTO membership and embrace globalization, liberalization, deregulation and privatization

The Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity (2006): the Supreme Court-sponsored international event that led to the 'Manila Declaration' and Canadian CJ Beverley McLachlin's proposal to rename the philosophy 'liberty and prosperity under the rule of law'
sub_topics: Opening lawyer-and-economist jokes: 'as many opinions as there are lawyers in the room' -- may have inspired Shakespeare to propose 'kill all the lawyers'; economists said to suffer the same opinionated excess, though Shakespeare only mentioned lawyers
The 'Momentum' book's blue cover: distinguished from maroon or green; understandable even by 'nincompoop lawyers'

The five authors as a Supreme Court for economic matters: Romeo Bernardo, Calixto Chikiamco, Emmanuel de Dios, Raul Fabella, and the late Cayetano Paderanga -- their pieces contain 'gems of thought tested by time then and now, by countries big and small, and by ideologies left and right'

Twin beacons thesis: 'humans need both justice and jobs; freedom and food; ethics and economics; peace and development; liberty and prosperity; these twin beacons must always go together; one is useless without the other'

The entrepreneurial-genius proof: 'The best way to conquer poverty, to create wealth and to share prosperity is to unleash the entrepreneurial genius of people by granting them the freedom and the tools to help themselves and society'

Tanada v. Angara (May 2, 1997): 'Filipino First' was the reigning economic doctrine; CJP had difficulty convincing colleagues; began with only three full concurrers; rest either dissented or concurred only 'in the result'; after 'days of patient explanations, discussions and deliberations' convinced all 14 others; unanimous decision

Quotation from Tanada: 'the Constitution did not intend to pursue an isolationist policy. It did not shut out foreign investments, goods and services... it allows an exchange on the basis of equality and reciprocity, frowning only on foreign competition that is unfair'

Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity (October 18-20, 2006): SC-sponsored with funding from World Bank, USAID, Canadian CIDA, European Union, Asia Foundation; ~300 jurists, academics and lawyers from around the world; Canadian CJ Beverley McLachlin proposed renaming the philosophy 'liberty and prosperity under the rule of law' to stress egalitarian goal via libertarian methods; Manila Declaration adopted -- calling for reconvening every three years

Post-retirement retreat by successors: after CJP retired, successors as CJ did not pursue the Global Forum initiative; Court returned to 'giving primacy to liberty and shelving prosperity as only a secondary objective'

Constitutional architecture: Bill of Rights -- mandatory, self-executing, no implementing legislation needed; prosperity provisions (education, healthy environment, freedom from poverty) -- in Declaration of Principles, Social Justice, Education articles -- generally viewed as 'mere ideals and aspirations,' not mandatory, not self-executing, requiring implementing laws

Historical reason: Philippine Constitutions born from centuries-old struggle for political freedom (Spain, America); borrowed US Bill of Rights from American battle for independence (Patrick Henry: 'Give me liberty or give me death')

FLP programs described: 20 professorial chairs (Metrobank Foundation), 20 legal scholarships at P200,000 each (Tan Yan Kee Foundation), first batch scholars copping 1st and 5th in bar exams, dissertation writing contest (Ayala Corporation, prizes totaling ~P2M)
FLP upcoming plans (as of 2019): roving Museum on Liberty and Prosperity in 2020; reconvening of Global Forum in 2021 (15 years after the 2006 first one)
The book's contribution: 'intentionally or unintentionally, immensely contributes to this valiant effort to equalize the war against poverty with the struggle for liberty'

stances.claim: CJP's liberty-and-prosperity legal philosophy is in 'legal equilibrium' with the economists' thesis in 'Momentum' -- the same truth reached from different disciplines (law vs. economics) using different tools (judicial decisions vs. econometric analysis). The book and CJP's philosophy are complementary, not competing.

stances.claim: The Bill of Rights is constitutionally dominant (mandatory, self-executing) while the prosperity provisions (education, healthy environment, freedom from poverty) are constitutionally subordinate (aspirational, requiring implementing legislation). This constitutional architecture is the structural reason for the persistence of poverty despite political freedom.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-architecture-as-poverty-cause: the legal design of the 1987 Constitution explains the liberty/prosperity imbalance

notable_anecdotes: Tanada v. Angara vote trajectory: in 1997, the 'Filipino First' doctrine dominated; CJP initially had only three full concurrers; others either dissented or concurred 'in the result' (agreeing with conclusions but not reasons); after days of patient deliberations, he finally convinced all 14 others for a unanimous decision -- 'more than two decades ago, the reigning economic doctrine was Filipino First.'

Canadian CJ McLachlin's renaming proposal at the 2006 Global Forum: 'the first female Chief Justice of Canada, Beverley McLaughlin (who recently retired at age 75), proposed in her major address, and I accepted, that the philosophy be renamed liberty and prosperity under the rule of law to stress that the egalitarian goal should be achieved only via libertarian methods.'

The Manila Declaration: the Forum adopted this declaration 'accepting and lauding the philosophy, and calling for a reconvening of the Forum every three years.' After CJP retired, his successors did not pursue the reconvening -- CJP's first indirect criticism of post-retirement judicial trajectory.

The constitutional architecture diagnosis: 'the reigning political rights, like the presumption of innocence... are mandatory and self-executing without need of implementing legislations. On the other hand, it listed the roads to prosperity... mostly in its three articles titled the Declaration of Principles and State Policies, Social Justice and Human Rights, and Education, Science and Technology... generally viewed as mere ideals and aspirations... not mandatory and self-executing. Verily, they need implementing laws to be judicially enforceable.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered October 23, 2019 at the book launch of 'Momentum: Economic Reforms for Sustaining Growth' (edited by Roel Landingin, with essays by Romeo Bernardo, Calixto Chikiamco, Emmanuel de Dios, Raul Fabella, and the late Cayetano Paderanga), this speech by CJP opens with the Shakespeare 'kill all lawyers' joke and declares that the book's authors -- 'if ever there would be a Supreme Court for economic matters' -- would easily constitute some of its most revered members. He proposes that his liberty-and-prosperity legal philosophy is in 'legal equilibrium' with the economists' thesis: the same truth reached from law (judicial decisions) and economics (econometric analysis). He then makes the constitutional-architecture diagnosis: the 1987 Philippine Constitution places political rights (Bill of Rights -- mandatory, self-executing, no implementing legislation needed) above prosperity provisions (Declaration of Principles, Social Justice, Education articles -- aspirational, not self-executing, requiring implementing laws), a design born from the centuries-old Filipino struggle against colonial domination (Spain, America) and the Patrick Henry 'give me liberty or give me death' tradition. He presents his most important economic ponencia -- Tanada v. Angara (May 2, 1997) -- where he had to overcome the reigning 'Filipino First' doctrine, beginning with only 3 full concurrers and eventually convincing all 14 other justices through 'days of patient explanations, discussions and deliberations' to unanimously uphold WTO membership and embrace globalization, liberalization, deregulation and privatization. He then describes the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity (October 18-20, 2006) -- SC-sponsored, funded by the World Bank, USAID, CIDA, EU and Asia Foundation, attended by ~300 international jurists -- where Canadian CJ Beverley McLachlin proposed renaming the philosophy 'liberty and prosperity under the rule of law,' and the Manila Declaration was adopted calling for triennial reconvening. He notes with regret that his successors as CJ did not pursue the reconvening and that the Court returned to prioritizing liberty over prosperity. He closes by describing FLP's programs (20 professorial chairs, 20 scholarships, dissertation contest) and announcing plans for a roving Museum on Liberty and Prosperity in 2020 and a Global Forum reconvening in 2021.
